analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC enforce antitrust law against tax-exempt nonprofit hospital systems.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors and has sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee since April 2025 with no action.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, the Federal Trade Commission can challenge anticompetitive mergers and conduct by for-profit companies, but tax-exempt nonprofit hospitals fall outside its reach, so large nonprofit hospital systems have grown through acquisitions with less federal antitrust scrutiny. This bill changes the FTC's definition so tax-exempt hospital organizations are covered. It would let the agency block or unwind hospital deals and practices that drive up prices for patients, employers, and insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and workers in areas dominated by one or a few hospital systems, especially where nonprofits have merged into large regional monopolies. If the FTC can police these deals, consolidation that raises prices could be stopped, and independent clinics and smaller hospitals competing against giant systems would get a fairer market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and workers in hospital-monopoly regions

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the FTC Act's definition of 'Corporation' to include tax-exempt hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations, closing a gap that has kept nonprofit hospital systems largely outside federal antitrust enforcement [S2].

Hospital markets are unusually concentrated, and FTC economists have found hospital mergers tend to raise prices; extending enforcement to the nonprofit systems that dominate many markets gives the agency a tool to challenge those deals [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large tax-exempt hospital systems, which would face antitrust scrutiny of their mergers and market conduct for the first time. Hospital deals that might otherwise proceed could be blocked, and systems would bear the cost of defending enforcement actions.

drawbacks.text: The bill only extends the FTC's legal authority; it does not itself lower prices, and enforcement would depend on the agency choosing to bring cases [S2].

Hospitals argue some mergers let small facilities stay open and share expensive equipment and specialists, so a blanket antitrust crackdown on nonprofit deals could block combinations that keep rural care alive [S2].
Covered systems would face litigation and compliance costs, which hospitals could argue pressure budgets for charity care and community services [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people facing few hospital choices and high medical prices, giving the FTC authority over nonprofit hospital systems is a real check on consolidation. The honest caveat is that this is an enforcement tool, not a price cap: it works only if the FTC acts, and some challenged mergers genuinely do preserve small-town services. On balance, closing the nonprofit loophole addresses one of the biggest unpoliced corners of health care consolidation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; no cosponsors have signed on.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill in the House on April 24, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the record shows no further action since [S4].
No other House members have cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large nonprofit hospital systems are better off so far: with no cosponsors and no committee action, the loophole that keeps them outside FTC antitrust authority remains open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nonprofit hospital systems avoiding FTC scrutiny

for.name: Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited no cosponsors on the record.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it in committee.

sides.party_line_note: There is no record of party positioning: the bill has a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote has ever been scheduled [S3][S4].

industries.note: For the first time these systems would face FTC antitrust enforcement of mergers and market conduct. Their interest in staying outside that authority runs against patients, since hospital consolidation raises the prices people pay.

Insurers pay hospital prices and pass them into premiums, so checks on hospital market power lower their costs. Ordinary workers with employer coverage share in that benefit, though savings only reach patients if passed through.
These providers compete with large systems that have absorbed rivals; antitrust oversight of the giants gives smaller players a fairer market and patients more choices.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a single sponsor and zero cosponsors rarely get a committee hearing, let alone a floor vote, in a busy Congress. Unless Rep. Spartz builds cosponsor support or hospital-antitrust concerns draw leadership attention, this bill will likely die in committee at the end of the 119th Congress.
